stem: Gauss's law states the electric flux through a closed surface is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: closed-surface flux depends on enclosed charge

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This mistakes ε₀ for a multiplier on the enclosed charge rather than the divisor Gauss's law requires.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This confuses charge outside the surface with enclosed charge, which contributes zero net flux.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This overgeneralizes the special zero-net-enclosed-charge case (or the magnetic-flux identity) into a universal rule.

stem: For a spherically symmetric volume charge density, the charge enclosed within radius R is…

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: integrate density over spherical volume elements

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This evaluates the density only at the outer radius and scales it linearly by R instead of integrating over the volume.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This drops the 4πr² spherical-shell area factor, treating the volume element as just dr.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This inverts the relationship, dividing a surface area by density instead of integrating density over volume.

stem: For electrostatics in one dimension, the x-component of the electric field is related to the electric potential V(x) by

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This drops the negative sign: the field points toward decreasing potential, so E_x = -dV/dx.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The field component is the negative derivative of the potential with respect to position.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This treats the field as the ratio of V to position, which would equal -dV/dx only if V were linear in x and zero at x = 0; in general the field is the derivative of V, not a ratio.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This substitutes a time integral for the spatial gradient, conflating a static field relation with time dependence.

stem: At a point on the x-axis where the electric potential V(x) has a stationary point (dV/dx = 0), which statement must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The field component E_x is zero there.
choices.rationale: Since E_x = -dV/dx, a stationary point of V, where dV/dx = 0, has E_x = 0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The potential V must equal zero there.
choices.rationale: This confuses a vanishing slope of V with the value of V itself being zero; V can have any value at a maximum or minimum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An infinite charge must be located there.
choices.rationale: A stationary point requires only that the slope of V vanish, not an infinite charge source.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The field component E_x must be nonzero there.
choices.rationale: This reverses the relation E_x = -dV/dx: a zero slope of V gives a zero field component, not a nonzero one.

stem: Capacitance of parallel plates neglecting edges is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: C=Q/ΔV=εA/d.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This swaps the positions of A and d in the formula.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This puts ε in the denominator and both A and d in the numerator; capacitance increases with plate area and decreases with plate separation, so A and d cannot both appear in the numerator.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This takes the reciprocal of the correct capacitance expression.

stem: Energy stored in a capacitor is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This drops the factor of one-half that comes from integrating V dq up to charge Q.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: integrating V dq gives one-half CV²

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This divides by V² instead of multiplying, inverting the voltage dependence.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This misplaces the factor of 2 as a coefficient of C divided by V rather than one-half CV².

stem: In electrostatic equilibrium, within the conducting material of a conductor, E is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This reverses the actual physics, assuming free charge concentrates the field rather than canceling it in equilibrium.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Free charges rearrange until the field within the conducting material vanishes.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This mistakes electrostatic equilibrium for merely uniform field conditions; equilibrium in a conductor specifically requires E to vanish everywhere within the conducting material, not merely be constant.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This assumes electrostatic equilibrium implies an oscillating field rather than a static zero field.

stem: Two point charges remain fixed while their separation triples. The force magnitude becomes

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies direct rather than inverse distance scaling.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses inverse-linear scaling and misses the square.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Coulomb force varies as 1/r², so tripling r divides force by nine.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This incorrectly uses an inverse-cube relation.

stem: The electric field due to an isolated negative point charge points

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the direction for a positive source charge.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The field points in the force direction on a positive test charge, toward a negative source.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This confuses electric point-charge geometry with magnetic field around a current.

choices.label: D
choices.text: its direction depends on the sign of the test charge
choices.rationale: Electric-field direction is a property of the source charge and does not depend on the sign of a test charge.

stem: For a line charge λ(s), the differential charge element is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Linear density times differential length gives dq=λ ds.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses an area element appropriate to surface charge density.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses a volume element appropriate to volume charge density.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The linear charge density already gives charge per unit length, so dq = λ(s)ds; differentiating λ is not required.

stem: Uniform E crosses flat area A whose normal makes angle θ with E. Electric flux is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses the angle with the surface rather than the stated angle with its normal.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Flux is the dot product EA cosθ using the surface normal.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This divides by the projection factor instead of multiplying.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This ignores the angle between the electric field and the surface normal; only the normal component contributes to flux.

stem: Charges outside a closed Gaussian surface contribute to

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This incorrectly counts external charge as enclosed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: local field but zero net flux contribution
choices.rationale: External charges can affect E locally, but their field lines enter and leave with zero net closed-surface flux.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This ignores the electric field from external sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: nonzero net flux but no enclosed charge
choices.rationale: An external charge's field lines enter and leave a closed surface with zero net flux contribution.

stem: Two positive point charges are brought closer together. Their electric potential energy

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This reverses the inverse-distance dependence for positive U.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: For like charges U=kq₁q₂/r is positive and increases as separation decreases.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This assumes a zero reference means all separations have zero energy.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Negative potential energy applies to opposite-sign charges.

stem: With V(∞)=0, point-charge potential is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Integrating the point-charge field from infinity gives V=kq/r.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This has the 1/r² dependence of the point-charge field magnitude k|q|/r², not the 1/r dependence of the potential.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This incorrectly introduces a factor of one-half from energy formulas.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This incorrectly retains a negative sign; the potential is kq/r and its sign is determined by q.

stem: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field just outside a conductor is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This would drive free charges along the surface and violate equilibrium.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Any tangential field would move surface charge, so equilibrium field is normal.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Interior field is zero, but exterior normal field can be nonzero.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Electrostatic equilibrium has no sustained surface current.

stem: A dielectric with κ>1 fully fills a capacitor that remains connected to an ideal battery. Stored energy

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses the fixed-charge result instead of the fixed-voltage condition.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This ignores the capacitance increase while voltage is held fixed.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: At fixed V, C increases by κ and U=(1/2)CV² increases by κ.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: With the voltage held fixed by the battery, U = (1/2)CV² changes only through C, which increases by κ, so the stored energy increases by κ; the charge on the plates also increases by κ, but that is already reflected in the factor κ and does not produce an additional κ².

stem: An infinitely long, uniformly charged wire has linear charge density lambda > 0. Using Gauss's law with a cylindrical Gaussian surface of length L, which expression correctly gives the electric field magnitude at a perpendicular distance r from the wire?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The Gaussian surface's curved lateral area is 2*pi*r*L, and the enclosed charge is lambda*L; solving E*(2*pi*r*L)=lambda*L/epsilon_0 gives E=lambda/(2*pi*epsilon_0*r).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the 1/r² dependence of a spherically symmetric (point-charge) field, which does not apply to a long cylindrical charge distribution, whose field falls off as 1/r.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This leaves the length L in the answer; the enclosed charge λL and the lateral area 2πrL both contain L, so it cancels and the field cannot depend on the arbitrary length of the Gaussian cylinder.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This has the wrong r-dependence (1/r² instead of 1/r) and the wrong numerical factor; the lateral area of the cylinder is 2πrL, giving E = λ/(2πε₀r).

stem: A thin spherical shell of radius R carries total charge +Q uniformly distributed on its surface. Using a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r, where r > R, what is the correct enclosed charge q_enc to use in Gauss's law?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Since r > R, the entire charged shell (all of charge Q, physically located at radius R) lies inside the Gaussian surface, regardless of how much larger r is than R.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This incorrectly scales the enclosed charge with the Gaussian surface's radius, as though charge were spread out to fill the larger radius -- a documented misconception.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This incorrectly scales the enclosed charge inversely with the Gaussian radius; the physical charge does not change based on where the imaginary Gaussian surface is drawn.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This incorrectly assumes no charge is enclosed, but the shell's charge lies entirely within any Gaussian surface of radius r > R.

stem: In a region of space, the electric potential decreases as x increases (dV/dx < 0 everywhere in this region). What can be concluded about the electric field component E_x in this region?

choices.label: A
choices.text: E_x is positive (the field points in the +x direction)
choices.rationale: Since E_x = -dV/dx, and dV/dx is negative, E_x = -(negative) = positive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: E_x is negative (the field points in the -x direction)
choices.rationale: This drops the negative sign in E_x=-dV/dx, incorrectly keeping the same sign as dV/dx instead of flipping it.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: A nonzero (negative) spatial rate of change in potential corresponds to a nonzero field component, not zero.

choices.label: D
choices.text: E_x cannot be determined without more information
choices.rationale: The relationship E_x=-dV/dx directly determines the sign of E_x from the sign of dV/dx alone.

stem: A charge +Q is fixed at one location, and a charge -Q of equal magnitude is fixed a distance away. At the midpoint between them, which statement is correct? (Use the standard convention V=0 at infinity.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: The electric field is nonzero, but the electric potential is zero
choices.rationale: At the midpoint, both charges' field contributions point in the same direction (from + toward -) and add, giving a nonzero field; but the potential contributions are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign (+kQ/r and -kQ/r), summing to exactly zero.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The electric field is zero, but the electric potential is nonzero
choices.rationale: This reverses the correct result -- the field components add (same direction) rather than cancel, and the potential terms cancel (opposite signs) rather than add.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both the electric field and electric potential are zero
choices.rationale: The field does not cancel here, since both contributions point in the same direction at the midpoint.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both the electric field and electric potential are nonzero
choices.rationale: The potential does cancel exactly, since the two equal-and-opposite charges are equidistant from the midpoint.

stem: A solid insulating sphere of radius R has uniform volume charge density rho. What is the electric field magnitude at a distance r = R/2 from the center (inside the sphere)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Inside a uniformly charged sphere, E(r)=rho*r/(3*epsilon_0). At r=R/2, this gives rho*(R/2)/(3*epsilon_0)=rho*R/(6*epsilon_0).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses r=R (the surface value) instead of the requested interior point r=R/2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is half the correct value, as if the factor of 1/2 from r = R/2 were applied a second time to ρr/(3ε₀).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This omits the factor of 1/3: Gauss's law gives E(4πr²) = ρ(4/3)πr³/ε₀, so E = ρr/(3ε₀), not ρr/ε₀; the incorrect form ρr/ε₀ evaluates to ρR/(2ε₀) at r = R/2.

stem: A charged conductor is in electrostatic equilibrium. Which statement correctly describes the electric field at a point just inside the conductor's surface, and at a point just outside its surface? (Assume the point in question lies on a region of the surface where the local surface charge density is nonzero.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zero just inside; nonzero and perpendicular to the surface just outside
choices.rationale: In electrostatic equilibrium, the field inside a conductor is always zero, and just outside a charged conductor's surface the field is nonzero and perpendicular to the surface.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nonzero just inside; zero just outside
choices.rationale: This reverses the correct relationship -- the field is zero inside a conductor in equilibrium, not outside it.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The field just outside a charged conductor's surface is nonzero.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonzero and parallel to the surface at both locations
choices.rationale: The field inside a conductor in equilibrium is zero, not nonzero and parallel to the surface.

stem: A point charge +Q sits at the exact center of a cubical Gaussian surface. What is the electric flux through one face of the cube?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: By Gauss's law the total flux through the cube is Q/epsilon_0; by symmetry, the six identical faces each receive an equal share, giving Q/(6*epsilon_0) per face.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is the TOTAL flux through the entire cube, not the flux through just one face.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is the flux through a portion of the surface that subtends one steradian (the total flux divided by 4π), not the flux through one face of the cube; a cube face subtends 4π/6 steradians as seen from the center.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This divides by an incorrect number of faces (24 instead of 6).

stem: A positive charge is released from rest and acted on only by a static electric field. It tends toward

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This sends the charge uphill in potential energy without external work.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: For q>0, U=qV, so electric force accelerates it toward lower V and lower U.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: For positive charge, higher V means higher, not lower, potential energy.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: A potential-energy decrease generally appears as increased kinetic energy.
